served.bankWhy: Pumps push uphill and turbines run downhill. The electron carriers load protons into the lumen, so the lumen becomes the crowded acidic side, and ATP synthase lets that crowd stream back out into the stroma. The ATP shows up exactly where the Calvin cycle needs it, which makes a handy sanity check.

answer.text: From the lumen into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
answer.line: Protons crowd the lumen and flow back out through ATP synthase. Its head faces the stroma, so ATP appears there.

steps: Find where the protons pile up. Water splitting and cytochrome b6f load H+ into the thylakoid lumen.
Pumps push uphill; the turbine runs downhill. H+ flows down its gradient through ATP synthase, out of the lumen into the stroma.
Check where the head sits. It sticks into the stroma, so ATP is made right where the Calvin cycle spends it.

choices.text: From the stroma into the lumen, with the ATP appearing in the lumen
choices.note: Stroma to lumen is the way the carriers pump H+, uphill. Through the synthase H+ runs the other way, and ATP never appears in the lumen.

choices.text: From the cytosol into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
choices.note: The cytosol sits outside the chloroplast and is not part of this gradient. This borrows an outside-to-inside layout like the mitochondrion's.

choices.text: From the lumen into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the lumen
choices.note: The proton direction is right. But the head of the enzyme faces the stroma, so the ATP is released there.

choices.text: From the lumen into the stroma, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
choices.note: Downhill out of the lumen; ATP made in the stroma, next to the Calvin cycle.

choices.text: From the stroma into the lumen, with the ATP appearing in the stroma
choices.note: ATP does appear in the stroma. But H+ moves through the synthase down its gradient, out of the lumen, not into it.

visual.alt: A slice of thylakoid membrane with the stroma above and the lumen below. Electrons run from water through photosystem II, cytochrome b6f and photosystem I to NADPH, while water splitting and b6f load H+ into the lumen; ATP synthase, outlined as the answer, lets H+ flow back up into the stroma, where its head makes ATP.
